summary: Specifies tools for monitoring a chain of Path Computation Elements (PCEs), the servers that compute traffic-engineered paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It extends the Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) so operators can check whether each PCE is alive, spot resource contention, and gather path computation time statistics.

plainLanguage.summary: When many helpers pass a map question along a chain, someone needs to check that each helper is awake and how long they take. This adds a way to ask them.

questions: what is a path computation chain
subtitle: Extensions to PCEP that let operators check liveness, overload and processing times along a chain of path computation servers.

tldr.problem: When several Path Computation Elements (PCEs) cooperate to compute a path, the client usually sees only the first one, so it cannot tell whether the others are alive, overloaded or slow.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two PCEP messages (PCMonReq and PCMonRep) and new objects (MONITORING, PCC-ID-REQ, PCE-ID, PROC-TIME, OVERLOAD) that gather these metrics along the chain, either alone or alongside a normal path request.
tldr.outcome: Operators get tools for troubleshooting and performance monitoring of PCE chains, plus guidance on reacting to overload without making it worse.

today: RFC 5886 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the definition of PCEP monitoring. It extends the base protocol in RFC 5440.

sections.title: Why Monitor a Path Computation Chain
sections.content:
In a PCE-based network, a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute a Traffic Engineering label switched path (TE LSP) for MPLS or GMPLS. Sometimes no single PCE can see both ends of the path, so several PCEs cooperate. The RFC calls the set of PCEs involved a path computation chain.

With one PCE, a PCC can check liveness with IGP extensions or PCEP Keepalive messages. With a chain, the PCC may only see the first PCE, for example under the Backward Recursive PCE-based Computation (BRPC) procedure. The RFC therefore defines ways to collect state metrics along the chain: booleans such as alive or congested, and performance metrics such as path computation time.
sections.plainLanguage: If a question passes through many helpers, you only talk to the first one. You need a way to find out how the others are doing.

sections.title: In-Band, Out-of-Band, General and Specific Requests
sections.content:
Metrics can be gathered in band, meaning inside a normal path computation request (for example, asking for the processing time of that request along with the computed path), or out of band, as a standalone request such as checking the liveness of a chain.

Requests are also either general or specific. A general request is not tied to a particular path request (for example, average CPU load on a PCE). A specific request relates to one path computation, such as the time to complete it for a TE LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask how a helper is doing while you hand over your question, or you can just call to check on them. You can also ask about their whole day or only about your one question.

sections.title: The Monitoring Messages
sections.content:
Two new PCEP messages handle out-of-band monitoring. The PCMonReq message (Message-Type 8) goes from a PCC to a PCE to gather metrics from PCEs on a chain. The PCMonRep message (Message-Type 9) carries the answer back.

Both must contain a MONITORING object. If it is missing, the receiving PCE MUST send a PCErr with Error-type 6 and Error-value 4. A PCMonReq also carries a PCC-ID-REQ object, and optionally a list of PCE-ID objects plus the usual request objects. If a PCE list is present it takes precedence over any dynamic way of finding the chain, and a request naming an unreachable next-hop PCE MUST be silently discarded.

The P flag in object headers relates only to path computation requests, so it MUST be cleared in these two messages. For a bundle of requests, the MONITORING object SHOULD appear only in the first message and applies to the whole bundle.

A reply that is sent along a statically specified chain MUST use the same PCE list in reverse order.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a question card and an answer card. Each must have a header saying what you are asking about, and the answer goes back the way the question came.

sections.title: The Monitoring Objects
sections.content:
The MONITORING object (class 19) says which metrics are wanted, using flags: L (liveness), G (general request), P (processing time), C (overload) and I (incomplete, set by a PCE that supports the request but cannot provide any requested metric). It also carries a 32-bit Monitoring-id-number that, combined with the requesting PCC, identifies the request. It starts at a non-zero value and is incremented for each new request, while a resent request reuses the same number.

PCC-ID-REQ (class 20) holds the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the requesting PCC. PCE-ID (class 25) holds the address of a PCE, either to list PCEs to monitor or to record which PCE is reporting.

The PROC-TIME object (class 26) reports processing times in milliseconds: current, minimum, maximum, average and variance. Its E flag shows that the value was estimated rather than measured from a real computation. The OVERLOAD object (class 27) carries a 16-bit overload duration in seconds, the time the PCE expects to stay overloaded.

The RFC leaves the algorithms for minimum, maximum, average and variance up to each PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object is a small form: one says what you want to know, one says who is asking, one says which helper answered, one says how long they took, and one says how swamped they are.

sections.title: How PCEs Handle Monitoring Requests
sections.content:
A PCE that does not support PCMonReq answers with a PCErr (capability not supported). If it supports the message but policy forbids the request, it sends a PCErr with Error-type 5 and Error-value 6. A PCE may also partially satisfy a request, leaving out data that policy does not allow.

Otherwise the PCE decides whether it is the last PCE in the chain. If not, it relays the request to the next-hop PCE, which is either named by a PCE-ID object or found by a mechanism outside this document. The last PCE creates the reply. Each PCE on the way back adds its own objects and forwards the reply upstream. The same flow applies to a PCReq and PCRep that carry monitoring data in band.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper either passes the question on or, if they are last in line, answers. On the way back, everyone adds their own note.

sections.title: Manageability and Overload Thrashing
sections.content:
Implementations MUST allow monitoring to be switched on and off, and SHOULD allow configuring which kinds of requests (specific, general, in-band, out-of-band) and which metrics are allowed, per session or per group of peers. Because monitoring messages cost the PCE work, implementations SHOULD allow limiting their rate and handling PCReq messages at higher priority than PCMonReq.

The RFC also warns about overload thrashing: moving a queue from an overloaded PCE to another one can just spread the overload. It RECOMMENDS that a PCC does not cancel a queued PCReq and reissue it elsewhere just because the PCE is overloaded. A PCC that picks a different PCE for a new request should consider whether that one is or might become overloaded, and should not switch back without knowing the first PCE has recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: If one helper is swamped, everyone running to a different helper just swamps that one too. Better to wait a bit and check before moving.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Monitoring data can be abused. The RFC gives a denial-of-service example: faking overload information (the C bit and overload duration) to stop PCCs from using a PCE. It recommends using the PCEP security mechanisms from RFC 5440 to protect the new messages and objects, and says implementations SHOULD allow limiting the rate at which monitoring requests from a peer, or from another domain, are processed.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could lie and say a helper is busy so nobody asks them. Locking the line between helpers and limiting how often you can ask helps prevent that.
